newsitem.title: USA: Anti-semitic "Franklin" text surfaces on Internet.
newsitem.headline: Anti-semitic "Franklin" text surfaces on Internet.

text.p: An anti-Semitic text spuriously attributed to Benjamin Franklin has been posted on the Internet by computer-savvy neo-Nazis, the Franklin Institute said on Wednesday.
The museum said it has been deluged with telephone calls about the document known as "Franklin's Prophecy" ever since the text found its way onto the worldwide computer network.

The text, which has been in circulation since the 1930s, is purported to be from the diary of a South Carolina delegate to the Constitutional Convention and attributes a number of virulent remarks about Jews to Franklin.

Historians loudly declared the text a hoax soon after its appearance in 1934 in an American pro-Nazi publication called "Liberation," which claimed the original document was at the Franklin Institute.

Despite repeated condemnation from scholars, the text was cited by propagandists in Nazi Germany during the 1930s and 1940s, and has continued to make the rounds among members of the Ku Klux Klan and other American neo-Nazi groups.
More recently, extremists linked to the white supremacist National Alliance have begun posting quotations from the so-called Franklin Prophecy to some Internet bulletin boards.
There also have been reports of the text becoming Net-based propaganda for Islamic militants sympathetic to the Palestinian organisation Hamas.

"There has always been a trickle of calls about this text. It's one of those things that never dies. But in the last year or so, there has been quite a bit of activity on the Internet, and calls about it have increased substantially," Franklin Institute spokeswoman Elaine Wilner said.

Franklin was a major figure in in colonial America as a printer, publisher, inventor, author, scientist and statesman. He helped draft the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution, and also served as ambassador to France.
